analyzed-feature.name: Analyze, plan & build

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Map the code the request will change so the plan can be precise.
1. Find the entry points and modules involved, and follow the real data and control flow through them.
2. Identify the change surface: the files and symbols that must change, the callers and consumers affected, and any configuration, schema or persisted data involved.
3. Find the patterns to follow: how similar features are built here, naming, error handling and test style. Point at concrete examples.
4. List the tests that cover this area, the commands that run them, and where new tests belong.
5. Name the risks: compatibility, migrations, concurrency, performance, security, and areas you could not make sense of.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next and builds the plan on it, so reference concrete files and symbols and keep facts apart from assumptions.

analyzed-feature.description: Builds a change in code that should be understood first: Analyze maps the code and the change surface, Plan writes the plan you approve, Build implements it, and Verify checks every criterion and sends failures back to Build.

focus.plan: Build the plan on the analysis: use its change surface, the patterns it points at and the test locations it found.

implement.name: Build & verify

route.when: The user clearly approves going ahead and wants the change made now: 'do it', 'go ahead and build that', or a specific, already-decided change. This edits files.

implement.description: For a change that is already decided, often a plan from an earlier workflow: Plan adopts or completes it, you approve it, Build implements it, and Verify checks every criterion and sends failures back to Build.

focus.plan: This workflow usually starts once the change is decided. If the context already holds a plan or design the user agreed to (from Architect & plan, Debug & plan a fix or Security audit & fix plan), adopt it: keep its requirements, criteria, tasks and ids, and change only what the code shows is out of date or missing. Otherwise write the plan from the request.

documentation.name: Write documentation

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Find what documentation is needed and what it must say.
1. Identify the audience (users, contributors, operators, API consumers) and what they need to do with the docs.
2. Find the existing documentation: where it lives, its format and conventions, and what is outdated or missing.
3. Find the source of truth for everything to be documented: the symbols, commands, options, configuration and defaults in the code.
4. List the examples the docs need and how each can be checked (a command to run, a test, a compile).
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next; reference concrete files and symbols.

documentation.description: Writes or updates documentation from the code itself: Analyze finds the gaps and the source of truth, Plan lists what to write for your approval, the docs are written, Verify checks them against the code, and a final review reads them as their audience would.

focus.plan: Name each document or section to write or update, where it lives and who it is for. Criteria include that every statement matches the code and every example and command works.
focus.build: Write for the audience in the plan and follow the existing documentation conventions. Check every statement, name, option and default against the code, and run or compile every example and command you include where you can.
focus.verify: Check every documented name, option, default and behavior against the code, and run or compile the examples and commands where you can. Wrong or stale documentation is fail.
focus.review: Read the docs as their intended audience would: accurate against the code, complete for the task they support, easy to follow, consistent with the rest of the documentation, with working links and examples. Inaccurate content is fail; style preferences are not.

refactor.name: Refactor safely

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Pin down what the refactor must keep.
1. Identify the code to restructure and the goal of the refactor in the request.
2. List the observable behavior and the public interfaces that must not change: functions and types other modules use, outputs, file and data formats, errors.
3. Find the tests that cover that behavior and the commands that run them, and name the gaps where behavior is not pinned by a test.
4. Find every caller and dependent of the code that will move or change.
5. Suggest a safe order of small steps that each keep the project building and the tests passing.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next; reference concrete files and symbols.

refactor.description: Restructures code without changing what it does: Analyze pins the behavior and interfaces that must stay the same, Plan splits the refactor into small tasks you approve, each task is built and reviewed on its own, Verify runs the checks, and a final review confirms behavior is unchanged.

focus.plan: Tests that pin behavior not yet covered come first. Every task keeps the project building and the tests passing, and behavior and public interfaces stay the same unless the request says otherwise.
focus.build: Keep observable behavior and public interfaces identical. Run the tests before and after your change; a test may change only for an interface change the plan names, never to make a behavior change pass.
focus.review: Confirm behavior is unchanged: compare the old and new code paths, check every caller still gets the same results and errors, look for dropped edge-case handling, and check the structure improved the way the request intended, with no dead code or leftover duplicates. A behavior change the plan did not call for is fail.

investigate.name: Research & analyze

route.when: The user wants to understand or investigate how some existing functionality works, or how a technology or approach compares, before deciding anything: questions like 'how does X work', 'what are my options for Y', 'where is Z handled'. Nothing needs to change yet.

research.name: Research
research.instructions:
Find out what the user needs to understand or decide, and gather the evidence for it.
1. Restate the question in one or two sentences and list the sub-questions that must be answered before the user can decide.
2. Look at the workspace first: what the project uses today (manifests and lockfiles for libraries and versions, configuration, existing patterns) and which constraints that sets.
3. Where the answer depends on how a library, API, standard or tool behaves, check primary sources: official documentation for the versions in use, changelogs, release notes, issue trackers. Note the version and date of what you rely on.
4. When there are several ways to go, compare them on what matters for this project: fit with the existing code, complexity, performance, security, maintenance, licensing and the cost of switching.
5. Recommend one option, say why, and say what would change your recommendation.
6. Keep verified facts (with a link or a file path) apart from inference, and list what is still uncertain.
Do not change any files. Analyze reads your findings next and maps them onto the code, so name the parts of the codebase your findings touch and the questions only the code can answer.

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Answer the user's question from the code, using the research as a guide.
1. Start from the request and from the questions Research left for the code.
2. Find the entry points and follow the real flow: callers, data structures, state, configuration and error paths. Read the code rather than guessing from names.
3. Answer the question directly first, then give the evidence: a file path and symbol for every claim, with short excerpts only where they make the point.
4. Relate the research to this codebase: which option fits how the code is built, what adopting it would touch, and what it would cost.
5. Call out risks, surprises and anything you could not confirm, and say how to confirm it.
Do not change any files. Your report is the workflow's final result and goes straight to the user, who may continue with a design or a plan from it, so it must stand on its own: lead with the answer and a recommendation, then the supporting detail.

investigate.description: Answers a question about the code or a technology without changing anything: Research gathers sourced options and a recommendation, then Analyze traces how the existing code works and answers the question with file-level evidence.

researched-feature.name: Research, design & build

research.name: Research
research.instructions:
Gather what has to be known before the feature is designed.
1. Restate what the feature must do, and list the open questions that need outside knowledge: libraries, APIs, protocols, standards, platform limits.
2. Check what the project already uses (manifests, lockfiles, existing integrations) so the options fit the stack and versions in place.
3. Research primary sources: official documentation for the versions in use, changelogs, known issues, reference implementations. Note versions and dates.
4. Compare the viable approaches on fit with the codebase, complexity, performance, security, maintenance and licensing.
5. Recommend one, with the reasons and the conditions under which another would be better, and list what is still uncertain.
Do not change any files. Architect designs the feature from your findings next, so give it the facts it needs: API shapes, limits, configuration and pitfalls.

architect.name: Architect
architect.instructions:
Design the feature in this codebase, using the research.
1. Start from Research's recommendation; depart from it only for a reason you state.
2. Read the code the feature will live in: modules, interfaces, the patterns used for similar features, and the tests.
3. Lay out the design: components and responsibilities, interfaces and data shapes, data and control flow, state, error handling, configuration, and how each part is tested.
4. Name the compatibility constraints and the boundaries of the change: which files and modules change and which must not.
5. Order the work into pieces that can each be built and checked on their own.
Do not change any files. Plan turns your design into small tasks, each built by a fresh builder that sees only its own task, so be concrete: real paths, symbols and types.

researched-feature.description: For a feature that needs outside knowledge and a design first: Research gathers sourced options, Architect designs the solution, Plan breaks it into small tasks you approve, each task is built and reviewed on its own, and Verify checks every criterion.

focus.plan: Follow the Architect's design and its order of work.
focus.build: Follow the Architect's design: its interfaces, data shapes and boundaries. If the code makes part of it impossible, do the closest thing that meets the criteria and say what differs.

optimize-performance.name: Optimize performance

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Find where the time or memory really goes, and how to measure it.
1. Identify the slow or heavy path the request is about and the code on it.
2. Find or define a repeatable measurement: an existing benchmark, a profiling command, a timed test or a script, with its input size and conditions.
3. If you can run it, record the baseline numbers together with the command. If you cannot, say how it should be run. Never invent measurements.
4. Identify the likely bottlenecks with evidence (complexity, repeated work, I/O, allocations, locking), ranked by expected gain.
5. Note the behavior that must stay the same and the tests that pin it.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next and sets measurable targets.

optimize-performance.description: Makes something measurably faster or lighter: Analyze finds the bottleneck and how to measure it, Plan sets targets you approve, Build measures before and after its change, and Verify checks the numbers and that behavior is unchanged.

focus.plan: Make the measurement part of the plan: a baseline task with the exact command, then the changes, then the same measurement again. Criteria state each target as a comparison with the baseline under the same conditions, plus unchanged behavior.
focus.build: Measure the baseline with the planned command before changing anything, then change the code, then measure again the same way. Report both numbers from real runs only; if a measurement cannot run here, say so and give the command.
focus.verify: Check that the before and after numbers come from the same command and conditions and meet the plan's targets, and rerun the measurement if you can. Run the tests to confirm behavior is unchanged. A claimed improvement without a real measurement is fail, unless measuring is impossible here: then it is manual.

security-remediation.name: Security remediation

audit.name: Security audit
audit.instructions:
Audit the requested scope for real, exploitable security problems.
1. Define the scope and its trust boundaries: who supplies input, what is trusted, where secrets and sensitive data live, what runs with elevated rights.
2. Check the classes of problem that apply: injection (SQL, shell, path, template), missing authentication or authorization, unsafe deserialization, secrets in code, logs or errors, insecure defaults and configuration, misused cryptography, SSRF and open redirects, missing validation at boundaries, and dependencies with known advisories for the versions in use.
3. For each finding give an id (S1, S2, ...), a severity (critical, high, medium, low) with a one-line reason, the file and symbol, the conditions under which it can be exploited, the impact, and a precise remediation with the check that proves it is fixed.
4. Mark each finding confirmed (you traced it in the code) or unverified (a pattern that needs a closer look), and do not inflate severity.
5. Say what you did not cover.
Do not change any files. Plan turns your findings into fix tasks next, and at the end a security acceptance step checks each finding by its id, so the ids must stay stable.

security-remediation.description: Finds and fixes security problems: a security audit ranks the findings, Plan turns them into tasks you approve, each fix is built and reviewed on its own, Verify checks every criterion, and a security acceptance step confirms each finding is really fixed.

focus.plan: Each confirmed finding becomes a requirement under its id (S1, ...) with an acceptance criterion that proves the exploit no longer works; fix the highest severity first. Rotating leaked secrets, deploying and rewriting history are follow-ups for the user, not tasks.
focus.build: Fix the root cause of the finding at the trust boundary, not only the one call site, and do not weaken any other control. Add a test that shows the exploit no longer works where that is feasible.

security-audit.name: Security audit & fix plan

route.when: The user asks whether code is secure, or wants vulnerabilities, risky dependencies, exposed secrets or unsafe configuration reviewed.

audit.name: Security
audit.instructions:
Audit the requested scope for real, exploitable security problems.
1. Define the scope and its trust boundaries: who supplies input, what is trusted, where secrets and sensitive data live, what runs with elevated rights.
2. Check the classes of problem that apply: injection (SQL, shell, path, template), missing authentication or authorization, unsafe deserialization, secrets in code, logs or errors, insecure defaults and configuration, misused cryptography, SSRF and open redirects, missing validation at boundaries, and dependencies with known advisories for the versions in use.
3. For each finding give an id (S1, S2, ...), a severity (critical, high, medium, low) with a one-line reason, the file and symbol, the conditions under which it can be exploited, the impact, and a precise remediation with the check that proves it is fixed.
4. Mark each finding confirmed (you traced it in the code) or unverified (a pattern that needs a closer look), and do not inflate severity.
5. Say what you did not cover.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your findings next and turns them into a fix plan.

security-audit.description: Audits the requested scope for concrete security risks, ranks the findings and plans how to fix them. Nothing is changed; the fix plan can be handed to a build workflow.

focus.plan: Plan the fixes in order of severity. Each confirmed finding becomes a requirement under its id (S1, ...) with an acceptance criterion that proves the exploit no longer works. Unverified findings become investigation tasks or follow-ups. Rotating leaked secrets, changing production configuration and rewriting history are follow-ups for the user, not tasks.

careful-change.name: High-risk change

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Map the change and its blast radius before anything is planned.
1. Find every place the change reaches: the code that changes, its callers and consumers, public interfaces, persisted data and its formats, configuration, background jobs and other services.
2. For each, say what could break and how it would show up.
3. Find what protects it today: the tests that cover it and the commands that run them, types, validation, feature flags, and the gaps.
4. Identify what must not change: behavior other code relies on, data compatibility, the public API.
5. Suggest the safest order of work, how to roll back, and what to test before and after.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your report next and splits the work into small tasks, so reference concrete files and symbols.

careful-change.description: For changes where mistakes are expensive (shared code, data, public interfaces): Analyze maps the blast radius, Plan splits the work into small tasks you approve, each task is built and reviewed on its own, Verify checks every criterion, and a final review looks for regressions before you confirm.

focus.plan: Keep every task small and safe on its own, and put tests that pin current behavior before the change that could break it. Make compatibility and rollback explicit criteria.
focus.build: Change only what your task needs. Keep public interfaces, data formats and behavior other code relies on unless the task says otherwise, and add or run tests for every path you touch.
focus.review: Focus on risk: callers and consumers that may break, data compatibility and migrations, error handling and partial failure, concurrency, and whether a rollback is possible. A regression or an unhandled failure path is fail.

plan-build-verify.name: Plan, build, verify
plan-build-verify.description: The everyday workflow for a change: Plan writes requirements, acceptance criteria and tasks; you approve the plan (your notes revise it); Build implements it; Verify checks every criterion against the workspace and sends failures back to Build; checks only a person can do are given to you to confirm.

check-changes.name: Verify & review changes

route.when: The user wants work that was already done, their own changes or the previous result, checked or reviewed for correctness, regressions and quality, without anything being edited.

verify.name: Verify
verify.instructions:
Run the checks that apply to the changes and give the final verdict.
1. Run the project's checks that cover the changed code (tests, type check, lint, build) with the tools you have: focused tests for the changed areas first, then the wider suite when that is practical.
2. Report each check with the command, whether it passed, and the output that matters. Tell failures the changes caused apart from failures that were already there.
3. Confirm or refute what Review asked you to check.
4. Give the verdict: acceptable, acceptable after fixes, or not acceptable, with Review's blocking findings and any failing checks first.
Do not edit files. Your report is the workflow's final result for the user.

review.name: Review
review.instructions:
Review the changes the user means, without editing anything.
1. Work out which changes are meant: the ones the request names, the result of the previous workflow in the context, or the uncommitted changes in the workspace. Look at the actual code with the tools you have, and say which changes you reviewed.
2. Read every changed file and enough of the surrounding code to judge the change: callers, tests, configuration.
3. Look for wrong behavior and missed edge cases, regressions for existing callers, missing or weak tests, poor error handling, security problems, performance traps, and code that does not follow the project's conventions.
4. Give prioritized findings (blocking, should fix, minor), each with file and line, what is wrong, why it matters, and the fix.
5. Say whether the changes are acceptable as they are.
Verify runs the project's checks next and gives the final verdict with your findings, so list anything it should confirm by running a check.

check-changes.description: Reviews work that is already done (your own changes or the previous result) for correctness, regressions and quality, then runs the project's checks. Nothing is edited; you get prioritized findings and a verdict.

diagnose.name: Debug & plan a fix

route.when: Something is broken or failing and the user wants the cause found: an error message, a failing test, wrong behavior or a regression. A fix plan is wanted, not yet the fix itself.

debug.name: Debug
debug.instructions:
Find the root cause of the failure the user reports.
1. Pin down the symptom: the exact error, failing test, input or behavior, and what was expected instead. Take it from the request and the context; ask the user only if you cannot go on without it.
2. Reproduce it with the smallest check you can: one test, one command, one input. Record the command and its output. If you cannot reproduce it, say what you tried and what is missing.
3. Trace from the symptom to the cause: read the code on the failing path, form hypotheses, and test each against evidence (outputs, logs, code paths). Keep what you observed apart from what you suspect.
4. State the root cause with file and line, why it produces the symptom, and since when if that is visible (a recent change, a dependency update).
5. Specify the regression test: where it goes, what it does, and that it fails today and should pass after the fix.
6. Note other places with the same defect, and what the fix must not break.
Do not edit files or install dependencies; describe the fix instead. Plan reads your diagnosis next and turns it into the fix plan.

diagnose.description: Finds the cause of a failure (an error, a failing test, wrong behavior) by reproducing it, then plans the fix and its regression test. Nothing is changed yet.

focus.plan: Plan the fix for the root cause in the diagnosis, not a workaround for the symptom. The first task adds the regression test the diagnosis specifies (it fails today), the next fixes the cause, and the plan covers the other occurrences the diagnosis found. One criterion is that the regression test passes.

design.name: Architect & plan

route.when: The user has a requirement or earlier findings and wants a design or an ordered implementation plan before any code is written: 'how should we build X', 'plan this', 'design the approach'. Often the follow-up after an investigation.

architect.name: Architect
architect.instructions:
Design how the request should be built in this codebase.
1. Restate the goal, the constraints the user gave, and the decisions already made in the context.
2. Read the code the design will live in: the modules, their interfaces, the patterns used for similar features, and the tests.
3. Lay out the design: components and their responsibilities, interfaces and data shapes, data and control flow, where state lives, error and failure handling, and how each part is tested.
4. Where there is a real choice, compare at least two approaches and explain the one you pick: why it fits this codebase, what it costs, what it rules out.
5. Name the compatibility constraints (public APIs, persisted data, configuration, migrations) and the boundaries of the change: which files and modules change and which must not.
Do not change any files. Plan reads your design next and turns it into requirements and ordered tasks, so be concrete: real paths, symbols and types, not generic advice.

design.description: Turns a requirement or earlier findings into a design and an ordered implementation plan before any code is written. Nothing is changed; the plan can be handed to Build & verify.

focus.plan: Turn the Architect's design into the plan and keep its choices. Where the code contradicts part of the design, say so and plan what the code allows.

bug-fix.name: Fix a bug

debug.name: Debug
debug.instructions:
Find the root cause of the failure the user reports.
1. Pin down the symptom: the exact error, failing test, input or behavior, and what was expected instead. Take it from the request and the context; ask the user only if you cannot go on without it.
2. Reproduce it with the smallest check you can: one test, one command, one input. Record the command and its output. If you cannot reproduce it, say what you tried and what is missing.
3. Trace from the symptom to the cause: read the code on the failing path, form hypotheses, and test each against evidence (outputs, logs, code paths). Keep what you observed apart from what you suspect.
4. State the root cause with file and line, why it produces the symptom, and since when if that is visible (a recent change, a dependency update).
5. Specify the regression test: where it goes, what it does, and that it fails today and should pass after the fix.
6. Note other places with the same defect, and what the fix must not break.
Do not edit files or install dependencies; describe the fix instead. Plan writes the fix plan from your diagnosis next, and Build implements it.

bug-fix.description: Fixes a failure end to end: Debug reproduces it and finds the root cause, Plan writes the fix and its regression test for you to approve, Build adds the test and fixes the code, and Verify confirms the test passes and nothing else broke.

focus.plan: Plan the fix for the root cause in the diagnosis, not a workaround for the symptom. The first task adds the regression test the diagnosis specifies (it fails today), the next fixes the cause, and the plan covers the other occurrences the diagnosis found. One criterion is that the regression test passes.
focus.build: Write the regression test first and run it to see it fail for the reason in the diagnosis. Then fix the root cause, run it again to see it pass, and run the tests around the changed code. Report both runs.
focus.verify: Confirm that the regression test exists, exercises the reported failure and passes; that the fix addresses the root cause in the diagnosis rather than hiding the symptom; and that the tests around the changed code still pass.

specify.name: Specify a change

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Understand the change, the people it is for and the code it touches, so the spec describes this project and not a generic one.
1. Read the context: the project file with its principles, the capabilities that already exist, the change record, and the current spec if there is one. The request may add notes from the person; they are the latest word and win over the file.
2. Establish the purpose: who needs this, what problem they have today, and what is different for them when it is done. Take the answer from the request, the context and the code. Describe the outcome for a person, not the mechanism.
3. Read the code the change would touch: the modules, public interfaces, stored data, the behavior the change must keep, the tests that show how it works today, and one or two similar features whose conventions the new behavior should follow (naming, error messages, permissions, defaults).
4. Read the principles in the project file and note each one this change touches. A principle the change would break is a finding, not a detail.
5. Sort everything you learned into three groups, and keep them apart:
   - Decided: stated in the request, the context or the clarifications of an earlier spec. These are not questions any more.
   - Assumed: a reasonable default you would take, with the reason (what the code does elsewhere, what is usual for this kind of feature). An assumption is written into the spec so the person can overrule it.
   - Unknown: only the person can answer, and the answer changes the scope, the security or privacy of the change, or what a user sees. Do not put here what the code can answer.
6. Name the capabilities the change touches, using the names of the existing ones, and say for each whether the change adds a requirement, changes one or removes one.
7. Judge the size. If the request holds several outcomes that could ship and be tested on their own, say so and propose the split, one line per change. A change that cannot be described in one sentence is usually two.
Report under these headings: Purpose, Users, Observed (real paths, names and what each shows), Principles touched, Decided, Assumed (each with its reason), Unknown, Capabilities touched, Suggested split (or "one change"). Mark what you observed apart from what you infer.
Do not change any files. The next step looks for what is still unclear, and the one after writes the spec from your findings, so be concrete: real paths and names, not generic advice.

clarify.name: Clarify
clarify.instructions:
Find what is still unclear before the spec is written, and settle as much of it as the code and the context can, so the person is asked only what only they can answer.
1. Read the Analyze report and the context again with the eye of someone who has to build and test this without being able to ask. Where would two careful builders do different things, or two testers write different tests?
2. Scan these categories and give each a status, Clear, Partial or Missing:
   - Scope and behavior: the user goals, what is explicitly out of scope, which users or roles are affected and how they differ.
   - Domain and data: the entities and their attributes, what makes one unique, their lifecycle and state changes, how much data to expect.
   - Interaction: the main user journeys, and the empty, loading and error states along them; accessibility and language where it applies.
   - Quality attributes: speed, scale and limits, reliability and recovery, what must be logged or observable, security and privacy (who may do what, what data is protected), and legal or compliance constraints when they exist.
   - Integration: outside services and other parts of the system the change depends on, how they fail, data formats coming in and going out, versions.
   - Edge cases and failures: invalid input, repeated or concurrent actions and how conflicts are resolved, rate limits.
   - Constraints and trade-offs: fixed constraints from the project or the request, and alternatives the request rejects.
   - Terminology: the same word used for two things, or two words for one thing. Pick one term.
   - Completion: whether every outcome can be tested, and how a person would know the change is done.
   - Placeholders: TODOs, undecided items, and vague words (fast, simple, intuitive, robust, secure) without a measurable meaning.
3. For each Partial or Missing item choose exactly one outcome:
   - Resolve it, when the code, the context or the project file answers it. State the answer and its source.
   - Assume it, when a sensible default exists and a wrong guess is cheap to fix. Usual defaults that need no question: error messages in the project's existing style, data kept the way similar data is kept now, the performance users expect of this kind of product, the authentication the project already uses, the integration style the codebase already uses. State the default and why.
   - Ask it, only when the answer materially changes the scope, the data, the security or privacy, what a user sees, or how the result will be tested, and no default is safe.
   - Leave it out, when it is about how to build (a library, a pattern, a task order): that belongs to the design.
4. Rank the questions to ask by impact times uncertainty, covering the most important categories first; an unresolved security or scope question beats two small ones. Ask at most five. Everything above that limit is assumed, or listed as deferred with the reason.
5. Write each question so it can be answered in a word or a letter:
   - A full question that ends with `?` and makes sense on its own; never a topic label or an id as the question.
   - One sentence on why it matters: what goes wrong for the users or the tests if it is answered wrongly.
   - Your recommended answer with a short reason, then the real alternatives as lettered options (two to five, mutually exclusive), or, when there are no discrete options, a suggested short answer.
6. If the context holds a spec with open questions and the request or notes answer some of them (for example "Q1: B"), mark those as resolved with the chosen answer, and say which requirements and criteria the answer changes.
Report under these headings: Coverage (each category with its status), Resolved (each with its answer and source), Assumptions (each with its reason), Open questions (ranked and numbered Q1, Q2, ..., in the format above), Deferred (each with why it was not asked).
Do not change any files. The next step writes the spec: it turns your resolved items into requirements and clarifications, your assumptions into stated assumptions, and your open questions into questions for the person, so be exact about which is which.

spec.name: Write spec
spec.instructions:
Write the spec of the change as the file spec.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use this structure and these headings, in this order:

# <Title of the change>

## Why
Why this change is needed and for whom, in a few sentences.

## What changes
What will be different when this is done, from the point of view of a user.

## User stories
- US1 (P1): As a <who>, I want <what>, so that <why>. Independent check: <how this story alone can be tried and shown to work>.
- US2 (P2): ...

## Requirements

### R1: <A requirement, as a short statement>
Capability: <capability name> (adds "<Requirement name>")
<One or two sentences of detail.>

- C1: WHEN <situation> THEN <observable result>.
- C2: WHEN <edge or failure case> THEN <observable result>.

## Success criteria
- S1: <A measurable outcome for users, with a number, and no technology.>

## Key entities
- <Entity>: <what it represents, its important attributes and its relationships; no storage details.>

## Assumptions
- <A default taken where the request was silent, and why.>

## Out of scope
- <What this change deliberately does not do.>

## Clarifications
- <date>: Q: <question that was answered>? A: <answer>.

## Open questions
- Q1: <question>? Why it matters: <one sentence>. Recommended: A, <reason>. Options: A) <...>; B) <...>; C) <...>.

2. Write what the system must do and why, for a reader who is not a developer: never how to build it. No languages, frameworks, libraries, files, classes, endpoints, tables or steps; those belong to the design, which is written next. A requirement that names a technology is almost always a design decision in disguise: state the behavior it is meant to give.
3. User stories are ordered by priority (P1 is the most important) and each one is a slice that could be built, tried and delivered on its own. Its independent check says how a person would see that slice work without the others. The first story is the smallest version worth having.
4. Every requirement has an id (R1, R2, ...) and at least one criterion (C1, C2, ... numbered across the whole file, never reused). A requirement states one thing a user can rely on; if it contains "and", ask whether it is two requirements. Say in its detail which user story it serves (US1, US2, ...).
5. A criterion is something a person who was not here can check: WHEN a situation THEN an observable result. Think like a tester; a criterion that two testers would check differently is not done.
   - Checkable: "WHEN the user saves an album with a name that is taken THEN nothing is saved and the message 'An album with this name exists' is shown."
   - Not checkable: "Albums are validated properly." "The page is fast." "Errors are handled gracefully."
6. Cover the cases that matter, not only the happy path: for each requirement think about empty input, a value that is already taken, a missing permission, a repeated or concurrent action, a limit being reached, a dependency being down. A requirement with only a happy-path criterion is usually unfinished.
7. Success criteria are the measurable outcomes of the whole change: measurable (a time, a count, a percentage), technology-agnostic, seen from the user's or the business's side, and verifiable without knowing the implementation. "Users can create and name an album in under 30 seconds" and "searches over 10,000 photos show results within 1 second" are good; "the API answers in 200 ms" and "the cache hit rate is above 80%" describe the implementation and are not. Leave the section out when the change has no outcome worth measuring.
8. Key entities are only for changes that involve data: name each thing the system keeps track of, with its important attributes, what makes it unique and how it relates to the others. Leave the section out when no data is involved.
9. The Capability line says which capability the requirement adds to, changes or removes, using the names of the existing capabilities where they fit and the quoted requirement name. When the change changes or removes a requirement, use the exact requirement name that capability has now. Leave the line out for a requirement that belongs to no capability.
10. Use the Analyze and Clarify results this way: what was decided and what was resolved becomes a requirement or a clarification; each assumption goes under Assumptions with its reason; only the questions that are still open go under Open questions, at most five, numbered Q1, Q2, ... in the format above, so the person can answer "Q1: B". If the code or the context answers a question, answer it in the requirement instead. Write "None" under Open questions, Assumptions and Out of scope when they have nothing.
11. Do not invent requirements the request does not need. Everything in the spec traces to the request, the context or the code; a feature that "would be nice" belongs under Out of scope or nowhere.
12. When the context holds a current spec.md, revise it instead of starting over:
   - Keep its ids and everything the person wrote or edited. Never renumber; a removed requirement keeps its id retired.
   - For each open question the notes answer, record it under Clarifications as "<date>: Q: ... A: ...", and apply the answer where it belongs: change the requirement, add or correct the criteria, the entity or the success criterion it affects. Replace any statement the answer makes wrong instead of leaving both; no contradiction may remain.
   - Use one term for one thing across the whole file; where you rename a term, write "(formerly "X")" once.
13. Before you reply, check the spec against this list and fix what fails:
   - Content: no implementation details; focused on what users need and why; readable by someone who is not a developer; every mandatory section filled in.
   - Completeness: every requirement is testable and unambiguous; every requirement has criteria for its edge and failure cases; the scope is bounded by Out of scope; the dependencies and assumptions are written down; at most five open questions.
   - Readiness: every user story is covered by requirements; every success criterion is measurable and technology-agnostic; ids are unique; nothing contradicts the principles in the project file.
Do not change any files; the spec is saved from your reply.

checklist.name: Checklist
checklist.instructions:
Write the quality checklist of the spec as the file checklist.md: questions that test whether the requirements are complete, clear, consistent and measurable, the way unit tests check code. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Read the spec the previous step wrote (in workflow_input.spec), the Clarify report, the project file with its principles, and the current checklist.md in the context if there is one. The request may add notes from the person, such as a focus ("security", "the API"); a named focus gets its own section and more items.
2. Understand what this checklist tests. It tests the writing, not the software. Each item asks whether the spec says something, says it precisely and says it once: "Are the limits on an album name specified?", not "Verify that long names are rejected". Never write an item that tests behavior, code or a running system: no item starts with Verify, Test, Confirm or Check followed by something the software does, and none mentions clicking, rendering, loading, endpoints returning codes, frameworks or algorithms. How the software is tested is Implement's job.
3. Write the items with these patterns: "Are <requirements of a kind> defined for <scenario>?", "Is <vague term> quantified with a value or a rule?", "Are <section A> and <section B> consistent about <thing>?", "Can <criterion> be checked objectively?", "Does the spec define <missing aspect>?", "Are <edge cases> addressed?", "Is <assumption> stated and justified?"
4. Cover these dimensions, as one section each, leaving out a section only when nothing in the change touches it:
   - Completeness: every user story has requirements; every requirement has criteria; the errors, empty states, permissions and limits a person will meet are stated.
   - Clarity: no vague words left unmeasured (fast, easy, intuitive, robust, many, large, appropriate); every term means one thing; every message the person sees is given exactly.
   - Consistency: requirements, criteria, stories, entities and success criteria agree with one another and with the project's principles; the same thing has the same name everywhere.
   - Measurability: each criterion is a WHEN … THEN that someone who was not here can check; each success criterion has a number, a rate or a yes/no outcome and names no technology.
   - Scenario and edge coverage: the main, alternative, error and recovery flows; boundaries (zero, one, the limit, over it); concurrent or repeated actions; what happens to existing data and existing users.
   - Non-functional: performance, security and privacy, accessibility, reliability and observability, each where the change touches it, with a target where one matters.
   - Dependencies and assumptions: outside services, other changes and capabilities it relies on; every assumption stated and plausible; open questions numbered, each with a recommended answer.
   - Scope: what is out of scope is said; the change does one outcome (or the Analyze report's split is followed).
   Add a section for a domain the change is really about when it needs closer questions than the dimensions above: User experience for a screen or flow, Interface for an API, command or file format, Security for data, accounts or permissions, Data for stored data and migrations, Performance for stated targets.
5. Make each item specific to this spec. Name the requirement, story or entity it is about, and end it with where it points in brackets: the dimension and the spec location (`[Completeness, Spec §R2]`, `[Clarity, Spec §S1]`, `[Consistency, Spec §US1, §R4]`), or a marker when there is nothing to point to: `[Gap]` for something the spec does not say, `[Ambiguity]` for something it says unclearly, `[Conflict]` for two places that disagree, `[Assumption]` for something it takes for granted. At least four out of five items carry a spec location or a marker. A generic item that would fit any spec is not worth a line.
6. Answer each item from the spec yourself. Tick it (`- [x]`) only when the spec plainly answers it, and point to where. Leave it open (`- [ ]`) when the spec is silent, vague or contradicts itself, and say in a few words what is missing after the brackets. Do not tick anything on the strength of the code, the Clarify report or what the design will surely do: only the spec counts. An open item is work for the person, so it must say what to add or decide.
7. Keep it to what matters: between 15 and 40 items for most changes, fewer for a small one. Merge items that ask the same thing, and put the gaps that would change what is built (scope, security, data, what a person sees) first in each section.
8. When there is a current checklist.md, revise it rather than starting over: keep the ids and the wording of items that still apply, keep every item the person ticked ticked unless the spec has since changed what it answers, re-answer the others against the new spec, and give new items the next free ids. Remove items the spec no longer has a place for.
9. Use this layout:
   - The title line `# Checklist: <change title>`, then one line saying what it tests and that `[x]` means the spec answers the item, so the person can untick an item they disagree with.
   - One `## ` section per dimension or domain, in the order above.
   - Each item on one line: `- [ ] CHK001 <question> [<dimension>, Spec §R2] <what is missing, when open>`. Ids run CHK001, CHK002, ... across the whole file, never restarting per section and never reused.
   - A last section `## Summary` with the counts (items, ticked, open, gaps, conflicts) and the three open items that matter most, by id, each with the one change to the spec that would close it.
10. Before replying, check your own list: every item is a question about the writing and not a test of the software, every item names something from this spec, the ids are unique and in order, every open item says what is missing, and each line starts with `- [ ] CHK` or `- [x] CHK` exactly, because the host counts them.
Do not change any files; the checklist is saved from your reply next to the spec. The open items are shown on the Specs page, Plan reads them as gaps to handle or name in the design, and the person closes them by editing the spec or running Specify again with notes.

specify.description: Writes the spec of a change into its folder: Analyze reads the project, the existing capabilities and the code, Clarify settles what the code can answer and ranks what only you can, then the spec is written with requirements, criteria, assumptions and open questions, and Checklist tests its quality with questions it ticks where the spec answers them (checklist.md). Nothing else is changed.

spec-plan.name: Design & tasks for a spec

architect.name: Design
architect.instructions:
Write the design of the change as the file design.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Read the context: the project file and its principles, the spec of the change (user stories, requirements, criteria, success criteria, entities, assumptions), the research if there is some, and any current design to revise. Decisions in Clarifications are made. For an open question the person has not answered, design for its recommended answer, say so, and keep that part easy to change.
2. Check the principles first, as a gate. If the change as specified cannot be built without breaking a principle, say so at the top of the design and propose the least harmful way; do not quietly design around it.
3. Read the code the design will live in before you decide anything: the modules and their interfaces, how similar features are built, the data they keep, the error handling and the tests. A design that ignores the pattern the codebase already uses needs a reason.
4. Resolve every unknown before you rely on it. When a decision depends on how an outside library, service or API behaves and the code does not show it, ask the Research step with request_research rather than guessing, and record what it found.
5. Use these headings, in this order:
   - `## Summary`: the main requirement and the chosen approach in three or four sentences.
   - `## Technical context`: language and version, main dependencies, storage, how it is tested, target platform, project type, and the performance goals, constraints and scale that apply. Take each from the code or the project file; write "unknown" and the assumption you make where neither says.
   - `## Decisions`: one entry per real choice, as "Decision: ... Rationale: ... Alternatives considered: ...". Compare at least two options where there is a real choice, by what they cost and what they risk, and say what would make you change your mind. Prefer the smallest design that satisfies every criterion.
   - `## Components and files`: what is added or changed, with real paths and symbols, how the parts talk to each other, which requirements each serves (R1, R2, ...), and what stays as it is. Name the folder layout when new folders are added.
   - `## Data model`: for each entity of the spec, its fields and types, what makes it unique, its relationships, the validation rules taken from the requirements (limits, required fields, allowed values, exact messages), its state transitions, and how existing data is migrated or stays readable. Leave the section out when no data changes.
   - `## Contracts`: each interface the change exposes to users or other systems (a public function, a command, an endpoint, an event, a file format, a screen's inputs and outputs), with its inputs, outputs, errors and compatibility for callers that exist today. Leave it out when the change is purely internal.
   - `## Failure handling`: what can fail, what the user then sees, and what is left in a consistent state.
   - `## Testing`: which test proves which criterion, by id (C1, C2, ...), at which level (unit, integration, by hand), and what existing tests must keep passing.
   - `## How to try it`: the runnable scenarios that show the change works end to end: prerequisites, the commands or steps, and the expected result of each. Refer to the contracts and the data model instead of repeating them; no implementation code.
   - `## Principles check`: each principle of the project file, and how this design keeps it.
   - `## Complexity`: only when the design breaks a principle or adds something the principles discourage (a new dependency, layer or abstraction): a table with what it is, why it is needed, and the simpler alternative and why it was rejected. Leave it out otherwise.
   - `## Risks`: what could go wrong, how likely, and how it would show, plus what is left unknown. Add `## Migration` when existing data, configuration or callers need to be moved, and `## Rollout` when the change cannot be switched on all at once.
6. Every requirement and criterion of the spec must be addressed by something in the design, and every part of the design must serve a requirement: if a component serves none, remove it; if a requirement has no component, the design is incomplete. Check the principles again once the design is complete.
7. Do not widen the scope: a refactor the change does not need, a new abstraction for one caller, and a library for what the code already does are not part of this design.
8. When a current design.md is in the context, revise it: keep what the person wrote and change only what the spec now requires.
The next step checks the spec and the design against each other, and then the design is broken into tasks, so be concrete: real paths, symbols and types, not generic advice. Do not change any files; the design is saved from your reply.

check.name: Check
check.instructions:
Check that the spec and the design agree with each other and with the project's principles, and that the spec is well written, before the design is broken into tasks.
1. Read the spec (user stories, requirements, criteria, success criteria, entities, assumptions, open questions), the design from the previous step, and the project file with its principles. This is a read-only review; read code only to confirm a claim the design makes. Never report a section as missing without checking that it is really absent.
2. Build an inventory: every requirement (R), criterion (C), success criterion (S) and user story (US) with its id, and every component, entity, contract and test the design names.
3. Run these passes and keep what you find:
   - Coverage: for each criterion, the part of the design that satisfies it and the test that proves it. A requirement or criterion with no component, a criterion with no test, a success criterion that needs work (a limit, a load, a security property) with nothing in the design for it, and a design part that serves no requirement are all findings.
   - Principles: any part of the spec or the design that conflicts with a principle of the project file. A conflict with a rule stated as MUST is always a Blocker, and the fix changes the spec or the design, never the principle.
   - Inconsistency: the design doing something other than the spec, or more; two parts of the design contradicting each other; an entity or a field in the design that the spec does not have, or the other way round; the same thing named differently in the two documents; names, types and paths that do not exist in the code.
   - Ambiguity: vague words without a measurable meaning (fast, scalable, secure, intuitive, robust), placeholders (TODO, ???, <...>), and criteria two testers would check differently.
   - Underspecification: a requirement without a measurable outcome, a user story without criteria, an edge or failure case the spec leaves open that the design must decide, and open questions the design silently depends on.
   - Duplication: requirements or criteria that say the same thing; say which wording to keep.
4. Rate each finding:
   - Blocker: breaks a MUST principle, leaves a core requirement uncovered, or would make the tasks build the wrong thing.
   - Important: a conflict or duplication between requirements, an ambiguous security or performance property, an untestable criterion, a missing test for a criterion.
   - Minor: terminology drift, wording, a small gap that does not change the order of work.
5. Write each finding as a row: an id (the category's letter and a number, such as C1 for coverage or P1 for principles, kept the same when nothing changed), the category, the severity, where it is (document and heading or id), what is wrong, and the fix in one line. At most 30 rows, most severe first; summarize the rest in a sentence.
6. Finish with the numbers (requirements, criteria, criteria covered by the design and by a test, as counts and a percentage; findings per severity) and a verdict: "Ready for tasks", or "Needs changes" with the blockers. When there are blockers, name the assumption each task must make to stay safe until the person fixes them. A finding about another repository (a linked change that is not ready, a contract it must keep) names the work to do there, so the tasks step can make it a task or a follow-up; it is not a condition on this repository's tasks. When there are no findings, say so and give the numbers.
Report under these headings: Coverage (criterion, design part, test), Findings (the table), Numbers, Verdict.
Do not change any files. The next step writes the task list from the spec and the design and reads your report, so each finding must be specific enough to act on.

tasks.name: Tasks
tasks.instructions:
Break the design into the ordered task list of the change as the file tasks.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly this format: phases as `## ` headings, each followed by one line saying what can be tried when the phase is done, then one line per task with its instructions indented below it:

# Tasks: <number> <title>

## Phase 1: Setup
Checkpoint: <what works when this phase is done>

- [ ] **T1** <Task title, naming the main file>. R1 (C1)
  <What to change: files, symbols, the pattern to follow, the tests to add, and how to check it is done.>

## Phase 2: Foundation
Checkpoint: <...>

- [ ] **T2** <Task title>. R2 (C3) after T1
  <Instructions.>

## Phase 3: US1 <story title> (MVP)
Checkpoint: <the story's independent check from the spec>

- [ ] **T3** <Task title>. R1 (C1, C2) after T2
  <Instructions.>

2. Organize by user story, so each story can be built, checked and delivered on its own:
   - Setup: only what the change needs before anything else (a dependency, configuration, a new folder). Leave the phase out when there is nothing.
   - Foundation: what every story needs and that blocks them all (shared types, storage, a migration). Leave it out when there is nothing.
   - One phase per user story, in the spec's priority order. The first story phase is the MVP: after it, the smallest useful version works end to end. Its checkpoint is the story's independent check.
   - A final phase for what crosses stories: the project's whole check (tests, type check, lint, build) and fixing what the change broke, documentation the design calls for. Leave it out for a change that touches one area.
   Inside a story, go from data to behavior to the surfaces that use it, with each test in the task whose behavior it proves, written before or together with the code; never a last task that adds all the tests.
3. Every task has an id (T1, T2, ... in order, never repeated), names the requirement (R) and the criteria (C) it satisfies, and lists the tasks it must come after with `after T1, T2`. Every criterion of the spec is named by at least one task, and every task names at least one criterion; groundwork names the first criterion that needs it.
4. A task is one coherent piece that leaves the workspace working and fits in one builder session: it compiles, its tests pass and nothing is half done. Do not split so finely that one task cannot be checked without the next, and do not join work that could be checked separately. Two tasks that change the same file are ordered with `after`.
   - Every task ends integrated, not only compiling: never a task that adds or changes a shared type, hook, store or module and a later task that wires its callers to it. The task that changes it also updates every caller, or keeps the old path working until a named later task removes it.
   - Size each task against the code before you write it: for every file it changes, look up how many files depend on it (repo_context with mode blast_radius on that file, or search for its imports). A task that changes more than about 4 files, or a file that about 10 or more files depend on together with new behaviour, is too big for one session. Split it: first the narrow change of the shared file with all its callers updated and no behaviour change, then the behaviour on top, each with its own check.
5. The instructions must let a smaller model build the task without exploring or deciding:
   - The files and symbols to add or change, taken from the design and checked against the code, and the existing code whose pattern to follow.
   - The exact constraints from the spec and the design, quoted, not paraphrased: limits, required fields, allowed values, messages shown to the user, error codes.
   - The tests to add, named for the criteria they prove, and the command that shows the task works.
   - What the task must not touch when there is a risk of overreach. Point at the criteria instead of repeating the spec.
6. Use the Check report: where it names a blocker or an important finding, write the task so the builder does the safe thing and says what it assumed. Do not hide a finding by leaving it out.
7. Do not add tasks for deploying, releasing or changing systems outside the workspace; list those as follow-ups in the instructions of the last task.
   - Work in another repository (a linked change, a contract its code must keep) is never a condition inside a task of this one. When this change depends on it, add it as a task of its own whose title names that repository, or, when it cannot be done in this workspace, list it as a follow-up of the last task. Never write a task that may not claim its criteria until another repository proves something: write what the task builds and checks here, and its criteria are judged on that.
8. When a current tasks.md is in the context, keep every task that is ticked (`[x]`) exactly as it is, keep the ids of the rest where they still apply, add new ids after the highest one, and change only what the spec and design now require.
Before you reply, check the list once: every task line starts with `- [ ] **T<n>**` and names its criteria; no cycle in the `after` links; every criterion covered; every task buildable in one session and integrated when it ends (no task leaves a structure for a later task to wire in, none over the size limit); the first story phase alone gives a working MVP. Do not change any files; the task list is saved from your reply.

spec-plan.description: Turns the spec of a change into its design and an ordered task list in the change folder: Design reads the spec and the code and checks the project's principles, Check looks for gaps and conflicts between spec and design, then Tasks breaks it into small tasks that name the criteria they satisfy. The files are the result; you can edit them before building.

implement-spec.name: Implement a spec
implement-spec.description: Builds a change from its folder: the unticked tasks of tasks.md are built one at a time (a step plan, a builder and a review for each), then Verify checks every criterion of spec.md and you try what only a person can check. Finished tasks are ticked in the folder as the work goes, so a stopped run continues after them.

focus.build: The tasks, criteria and design come from the change folder. Read design.md before you start and follow it where the code allows: its Decisions, Data model and Contracts are binding, and the constraints quoted in your task are exact. Where the code proves the design wrong, do the smallest thing that meets the criteria and start a line with "Design deviation:" saying what you did differently and why, so the person can update the design. If spec.md still has an open question that bears on your task, build for its recommended answer and say so. Respect the principles in project.md: they are part of the definition of done. Write the tests the design's Testing section assigns to your task before or together with the code, and run them. When your task adds tooling or generated output, make sure build output, caches and secrets are ignored by version control. Do not edit the specs folder: the host ticks tasks and writes the task documents.
focus.verify: Check every criterion of spec.md against the workspace, not only those of the tasks built in this run: report each under its id (C1, C2, ...). Check that the principles in project.md still hold for the changed code, that the design's Testing section was carried out, and that the success criteria (S1, S2, ...) that can be measured here hold; the ones that need a real environment are manual, with the steps from the design's How to try it section. Report every "Design deviation:" the builders made, so the person can update design.md. A criterion no task covered is a failure of the plan: report it as fail and say so.

start-specs.name: Survey the project

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Work out what this repository is and what it does, so the project file and the capability specs describe the real thing and not what its name suggests.
1. Read the request and the context. Any project file and capability specs that already exist are to be revised, not replaced; what a person wrote stays. If the repository has little or no code, the request is the description of the project to write the specs for: work from it, and say that nothing was verified against code.
2. Read the repository from the outside in: the README and other docs, the manifests and build files, the CI configuration, the entry points, the main modules and their public interfaces, the data they keep, the configuration, and the tests. Use repo_overview, repo_context and project_info where they help; for a large repository read the structure first and the details of the main areas only.
3. Work out the project's purpose and its users, its stack, and the real commands to install, build, test, lint and run it. Confirm a command by finding it in a manifest, a script or the CI configuration; do not guess one.
4. Find the conventions the code really follows (naming, structure, error handling, logging, testing, how modules depend on each other), and the principles it plainly keeps, such as a rule that every public function is tested or that errors are never swallowed. A principle must be testable and seen in the code in more than one place; leave out what is only a wish.
5. Group what the system does into capabilities: coherent areas a person would name (a feature area or a subsystem, not a layer or a file), usually between three and ten, fewer for a small project. For each one note its purpose, the folders or files where it lives, the behaviors it provides taken from the code and the tests, and what it depends on.
6. Note what you could not work out: parts you did not read, behavior that depends on a service you cannot see, generated or vendored code you left out, and anything that looks dead.
Report under these headings: Project (purpose, users, stack), Commands (each with the file that confirms it), Conventions, Principles (each with where you saw it), Capabilities (name, purpose, paths, depends on), Not covered. Mark what you observed apart from what you assume.
Do not change any files. The next steps write the project file and the capability list from your findings, so be concrete: real paths and names.

project.name: Write project file
project.instructions:
Write the project file as the file project.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly these sections:

# <Project name>

## Purpose
What this project is for, who uses it, and what it deliberately is not.

## Stack
Languages, frameworks and where the code lives (the folders that matter).

## Commands
How to install, build, test, lint and run it (the real commands, one per line, each with what it does).

## Conventions
Naming, structure, error handling, logging, testing: what a new change must follow to fit in.

## Principles
Rules every change is checked against. Few, and each one testable.

2. State only what the analysis supports. Commands must be the real ones; leave out what you could not confirm instead of guessing, and say "not found" for a command that does not exist.
3. Conventions are what the code shows, not what is generally good practice: if the project does not follow a rule, do not write it. Each convention should let a newcomer predict where a thing goes or how it is named.
4. Principles are the project's constitution: Check and Verify treat a broken one as a blocker. Write each as a declarative rule with MUST or SHOULD and a short reason after it, never a vague wish ("code should be clean"). They are the few rules that, if broken, make a change wrong: for example "every public function has a test", "errors carry the path that failed" or "modules do not import each other's internals". Three to eight, each one short, each one something a reviewer can check against a diff. A principle the code does not keep today is not a principle of this project; leave it out or put it in the conventions as a direction.
5. Keep it short enough to be read in full by every later step: it is added to the context of every change. Details of a capability belong in its spec, not here.
6. When the context holds a current project file, revise it: keep what the person wrote and change only what is wrong or missing.
Do not change any files; the file is saved from your reply.

survey.name: List capabilities
survey.instructions:
Propose the capabilities of the repository as a list the person reviews, as the file onboarding.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly this structure, one `## ` section per capability:

# Onboarding: capabilities of <project name>

Edit this list, then write the capability specs. Delete an entry to skip it; copy an entry to add one.

## <capability-name>
Purpose: <one sentence: what this part of the system is for>
Paths: `<folder or file to start reading>`, `<another>`
Notes: <optional: what is tricky, what must not be missed, what to leave out>

2. A capability is a coherent area a person would name: a feature area or a subsystem, not a layer (such as "utils") and not a single file. It is something a user, or another part of the system, relies on. Aim for three to twelve; fewer, broader ones for a small project. The name is a short lowercase word or hyphenated words and becomes the folder under capabilities/.
3. Test each candidate: could it be described by requirements a person can check? Could it change without the others having to? If two candidates cannot be told apart, join them; if one hides several different promises, split it.
4. Paths must be real: only list files and folders you saw in the repository, the ones where reading should start (the main module, its public interface, its tests). Two to five per capability is enough.
5. Notes are for what the next step could miss: a part that is easy to get wrong, behavior that lives outside the listed paths, what belongs to another capability, generated code to ignore. Leave Notes out when there is nothing to say.
6. Do not list tooling, build scripts or configuration as capabilities unless they are what the project is for. Leave out dead code, and say in Notes of the nearest entry when something looks unused.
7. Order the entries so the core of the project comes first and supporting areas after it.
8. When the context holds a current capability list, revise it: keep every entry the person edited or added, keep the names, and only add what the code now shows or correct what is wrong.
The next step writes one spec per entry, each in its own run that reads the code at the listed paths, so the list decides what gets specified. Do not change any files; the list is saved from your reply.

start-specs.description: Surveys an existing project: Analyze reads the repository (or, for a new project, your description), then the project file is written and the capabilities are proposed as a list in onboarding.md for you to edit. Nothing else is written until you ask for each capability's spec.

onboard-capability.name: Write a capability spec

analyze.name: Analyze
analyze.instructions:
Understand one capability of the system from its code, so its spec says what the system really does and not what its name suggests.
1. Read the context: the project file, this capability's entry in the survey (its purpose, the paths to start from and the person's notes, which win over your impressions), the other capabilities, and the current spec if there is one.
2. Read the code at the listed paths and follow it where it leads: the public interface (what other code and users can call or see), the data it keeps and where, what it calls and who calls it, its configuration, and its error paths. Read the tests: they show the intended behavior and the edge cases someone cared about. Stay inside this capability; leave the others' ground to them, and mention a hand-over at the boundary only.
3. List the behaviors the capability provides, each as something a user or caller can rely on. For each, note the normal case and the edge and failure cases the code handles or its tests check: empty input, duplicates, missing permissions, limits, errors from what it depends on. Write down the observable result, such as the output, the message, the stored change, not the way it is implemented.
4. Separate what the code does from what it only intends: a branch that can never run, a commented-out path, a TODO or a test that is skipped is not behavior. Note it as a doubt.
5. Note what you could not determine (behavior that depends on a service you cannot see, configuration that changes the result), so the spec does not claim it.
Report under these headings: Behaviors (each with the normal case, the edge cases and where in the code you saw them), Interface, Data kept, Depends on, Doubts. Mark what you observed apart from what you assume.
Do not change any files. The next step writes the spec from your findings, so be concrete: real names and the behavior of each, not how it is built.

spec.name: Write capability spec
spec.instructions:
Write the spec of the capability as the file spec.md. Your whole reply is the content of that file, starting with its `# ` title line: no introduction, no closing remarks and no code fence around it.
1. Use exactly this structure:

# <Capability title>

Purpose: <one sentence: what this part of the system is for>

## Requirements

### Requirement: <Name of the requirement>
<One or two sentences of what the system does.>

#### Scenarios
- WHEN <situation> THEN <observable result>.
- WHEN <edge or failure case> THEN <observable result>.

2. Describe what the system does now, as requirements a person can check, taken from the code and its tests: not what it could do, not what it should do and not how it is built. Do not write about the implementation (classes, functions, libraries), except to name in backticks a file where a behavior lives, and only if it exists.
3. Write the detail of each requirement as a normative sentence ("Album names SHALL be unique within a library"). A requirement is one promise to a user or caller, in a short name that stays stable, because later changes refer to it by that name (`changes "Name"` and `removes "Name"`). Name it for the behavior, not the mechanism: "Albums can be renamed", not "Rename handler".
4. Each requirement has scenarios in WHEN … THEN form, with a result that can be seen or measured: the normal case first, then each edge or failure case the code handles. Take the scenarios from the code and its tests; one the code does not support does not belong in the spec. Where behavior depends on configuration, write one scenario for each value that matters.
5. Keep it focused: a handful to a dozen requirements. Merge requirements that are one promise; split ones that hide several. Put the most important first.
6. A behavior you doubt, or cannot confirm from the code, is left out of the requirements and listed under a final `## Open questions` heading as one line each, so the person can decide whether it is intended. Write nothing under it when there is nothing.
7. When the context holds a current spec, revise it: keep its requirement names and everything the person wrote, and add or correct only what the code shows. Do not delete a requirement because you could not find it; list it under Open questions.
8. Before you reply, check the spec once: every scenario is observable, no requirement describes an implementation, names are unique and stable, and nothing is claimed that the code does not do.
Do not change any files; the spec is saved from your reply.

onboard-capability.description: Writes the spec of one capability from the code at the paths the survey listed for it: Analyze reads that part of the system and its tests, then the spec is written as named requirements with scenarios. One run per capability.
